Article Title: Meta joins OpenAI and Anthropic, says our AI model went 'wild', but adds: We are 'not really responsible as …
Article Text:
Meta becomes the third AI company to report such incidents

What Irregular said about Meta’s Muse Spark breach

Calls for transparency

Meta has confirmed that its Muse Spark model exploited a security vulnerability in a third-party service during cybersecurity testing, marking the company’s first public disclosure of a rouge AI incident. According to a report by Business Insider, in a statement, Meta said that the breach occurred due to a misconfiguration by Irregular, an independent firm it uses for model evaluations. The error allowed the model to access the internet during testing. Meta added that it learned of the incident when Irregular notified the company and is now investigating, promising a full retrospective once details are finalised.Meta’s disclosure makes it the third major AI company to report such incidents in recent weeks. OpenAI admitted that two of its models escaped test environments and hacked into Hugging Face, later self-reporting two additional lapses. Anthropic revealed that its Claude models had gained unauthorised access to external systems during testing. Hugging Face itself confirmed a breach last month, while other firms have faced similar rogue agent behaviour.Irregular, the testing company involved, said the incident was not a sophisticated cyberattack but rather an evaluation environment issue similar to Anthropic’s disclosure. “This did not involve a sandbox escape or a sophisticated cyber action. There are no current open issues,” a spokesperson said, adding that Irregular is preparing a white paper on best practices for containment and secure evaluations.The string of incidents has prompted calls for stronger AI safety regulation and mandatory disclosures. Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue told CBS that transparency is critical, urging companies to share “agent traces” to determine whether lapses stemmed from human error, system flaws, or AI behavior. Industry leaders like Box CEO Aaron Levie have warned these breaches highlight the “wild times” ahead, as AI agents demonstrate the ability to escape systems, discover vulnerabilities, and hack external platforms.
Article Summary: Meta's Muse Spark model exploited a security vulnerability in a third-party service during cybersecurity testing. The breach occurred due to a misconfiguration by Irregular, an independent firm it uses for model evaluations. Meta’s disclosure makes it the third major AI company to report such incidents.

Article Title: Scientists turn Sharks into real-time ocean observers, carrying sensors that can measure conditions for oceanographic, atmospheric and climate models
Article Text:
AI generated image

Researchers decode ocean heat that fuels hurricanes

Tagging executed like a ‘Pit Crew’

Researchers from University of Delaware are transforming how oceanographers (scientists who study the earth's oceans) track marine conditions by deploying specialised electronic tags that turn living sharks into mobile, real-time data collection hubs. The research project, led by marine scientist Aaron Carlisle, equips predatory fish with advanced sensors designed to collect water profiles across the US East Coast.Instead of merely tracking animal movements, the tags gather critical data on temperature, salinity and depth – feeding real-time information directly into atmospheric and climate forecast models. The research was published in journal Frontiers in Conservation Science.The primary goal of the tagging initiative is to map the upper layer of the ocean, known to oceanographers as the mixed layer. This upper column of water holds the thermal energy that directly feeds and amplifies hurricane strength.“This is the part of the water column that really drives hurricane intensity — warmer mixed layer equals stronger hurricane — as it holds the heat that feeds hurricanes,” explained Carlisle, a professor in the university's School of Marine Science and Policy.While oceanographers have deployed sensor tags on marine mammals like elephant seals in polar regions, sharks present a unique advantage for Atlantic storm tracking. They are abundant, widely distributed, and traverse key coastal corridors where major hurricanes develop and gain strength before making landfall.Researchers target migratory species that surface frequently, such as shortfin mako sharks, blue sharks, smooth hammerheads and juvenile great white sharks. Frequent surfacing is critical because the electronic tags must reach the water's surface to transmit cached environmental data up to orbiting satellite networks.The research team conducts offshore expeditions aboard the university’s research vessel, deploying baited lines 30 to 60 kilometres off the Atlantic coast. When a shark is brought alongside the vessel, the team executes the tagging protocol with extreme precision under strict animal welfare guidelines.“The tagging process itself is operated like a pit crew in an auto race,” Carlisle said, emphasising that the procedure typically takes under five minutes. Each animal undergoes a quick health check before being tagged on its dorsal fin. To protect the sharks long-term, the tags are secured using metallic components designed to naturally corrode and shed after a predetermined period.
Article Summary: Researchers decode ocean heat that fuels hurricanes. Tagging executed like a ‘Pit Crew’ Researchers target migratory species that surface frequently, such as shortfin mako sharks, blue sharks, smooth hammerheads and juvenile great white sharks. Frequent surfacing is critical because the electronic tags must reach the water's surface to transmit cached environmental data.

Article Title: Google Drive is ending Google Photos backup starting August 10: What settings users need to change before deadline to ensure not losing photos and videos
Article Text:
What is changing for Google Photos users

What to do to keep your Google Photos back up

Google has confirmed that its Drive desktop app will stop supporting automatic Google Photos backup starting August 10, 2026. The change means that the users who rely on Drive’s desktop client to sync photos and videos from their computers will no longer see a new media automatically backed up to Google Photos. The company said that this move is part of its effort to simplify backup tools and also focus on dedicated photo management via the Photos app. “Google Drive for desktop ends support for Google Photos backup on August 10, 2026. To stop backing up existing folders before this date, use these instructions. To continue backing up folders after this date, you must add photos & videos from Google Drive to Google Photos,” said Google.Currently, the Google Drive desktop app allows users to designate a folder on their computer to be automatically backed up to Google Photos, a convenient way to keep photo libraries synced to the cloud without manual uploads. From August 10, that automatic connection between Drive for desktop and Google Photos stops working entirely. Any folders still configured for this kind of backup will no longer upload new photos or videos once the cutoff hits.Importantly, this doesn't mean Google Drive or Google Photos themselves are shutting down. Regular file syncing through the Drive desktop app will continue to work exactly as before — it's specifically the automatic bridge that pushed photos from a Drive-synced folder into Google Photos that's being removed. Google has also confirmed that any photos and videos already backed up to Google Photos through this method will remain safely stored and won't be affected by the change.For anyone who wants to keep automatic photo backups running, Google is directing users to set things up directly through Google Photos instead of via the Google Drive desktop app. There are two main options:* Continuous folder backup: In Google Photos, using the "+" button, users can select "Back up folders" and choose the computer folders they want backed up going forward, similar to how the Drive desktop app worked before.* Import from Drive: Users can also import photos that are already stored in their Google Drive folders directly into Google Photos.It is important to note that unlike the old Google Drive desktop integration, backups set up through the Google Photos website only run while the Google Photos site is open in a browser, rather than happening automatically in the background — a change that some users may find less convenient than the setup they are replacing.For casual users who mainly back up photos from their phones, this change will likely go unnoticed, since phone-based backups through the Google Photos app are not getting impacted. But for anyone who has used a computer folder — say, images imported from a camera or scanned documents — as their primary photo backup pipeline via the Google Drive desktop app, the deadline is worth acting on now. Missing it won't delete any existing backups, but it will quietly stop new photos from being backed up until the new setup is in place.
Article Summary: Google Drive desktop app will stop supporting automatic Google Photos backup starting August 10, 2026. Users who rely on Drive’s desktop client to sync photos and videos from their computers will no longer see a new media automatically backed up to Google Photos. The company said that this move is part of its effort to simplify backup tools and also focus on dedicated photo management.

Article Title: Anthropic has an important message for Claude users: Starting August 14, auto mode will be the default ...
Article Text:
How the Claude auto mode works

How to get started with the auto mode in Claude

Claude creator Boris Cherny is also the fan of this feature

What it means for users

Anthropic has announced that its auto mode will become the default setting for its Claude Code platform starting August 14. This change will affect the Pro, Max and Team accounts. With this new change in place, the developers will no longer need to manually approve each actin that AI takes during programming tasks. Instead, Claude Code will automatically process unless an action is deemed ‘irreversible, destructive, or aimed outside your environment’. The company first introduced auto mode in March as a test feature designed to balance speed and control. In its latest announcement, Anthropic said testing showed auto mode to be safer than manual review — catching 89% of harmful actions compared to just 13.6% detected by human reviewers. The company noted that users tend to approve nearly all permission prompts manually, making automated oversight more effective.The company first introduced auto mode in March as a test feature designed to balance speed and control. In its latest announcement, Anthropic said testing showed auto mode to be safer than manual review — catching 89% of harmful actions compared to just 13.6% detected by human reviewers.The company noted that users tend to approve nearly all permission prompts manually, making automated oversight more effective.Claude doesn't reach for your mouse and keyboard right away. It first checks whether a connector exists for the job—Slack, Google Calendar, and a handful of other services are already wired in. If a connector handles it, that's the path it takes. Only when there's no direct integration does it fall back to controlling your screen.From there, it can open files, navigate a browser, type into forms, and click through menus—anything you'd do yourself. It always asks permission before touching a new application, and you can pull the plug at any point.The feature pairs with Dispatch, Anthropic's task-assignment tool that lets you delegate work from your phone. The combination is what makes the whole thing more than a novelty. Assign a task on your commute, and the finished output is waiting on your desktop when you sit down. You can also set recurring tasks—scan my inbox every morning, pull the weekly metrics every Friday—and Claude handles them on schedule without being asked again.The feature is available for Pro and Max subscribers. You need the Claude desktop app installed and running on macOS. The mobile app alone won't control your computer—but you can use it to assign tasks through Dispatch, which then execute on your desktop in the background.Claude Code Head Boris Cherny shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) that he and his team have been using auto mode exclusively for months, saying he “couldn’t imagine going back to permission prompts.” “The team and I use Auto mode exclusively, and have been for many months. I couldn't imagine going back to permission prompts! Really excited to get this out to everyone,” wrote Boris.Anthropic added that new safety features — including prompt injection screening and customizable hard deny rules — have been integrated to prevent data leaks and unauthorized actions.The update marks a significant step toward autonomous coding, reducing the need for human oversight while maintaining strong safety checks. For developers using Claude Code, the shift to auto mode is expected to streamline workflows and improve efficiency without compromising control.
Article Summary: Anthropic has announced that its auto mode will become the default setting for its Claude Code platform starting August 14. This change will affect the Pro, Max and Team accounts. The company first introduced auto mode in March as a test feature designed to balance speed and control. In its latest announcement, Anthropic said testing showed auto mode to be safer than manual review.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

Article Title: Microsoft warns travellers of attacks on hotel Wi-Fi; says: Hackers can record your video, audio, steal passwords; how to know and protect yourself
Article Text:
Microsoft cuts 4800 job

How ‘CaptiveCrunch’ hacker attack works

Microsoft revealed that the attacks takes place in two primary ways:

How travelers can stay safe

Microsoft’s Threat Intelligence team has issued a warning to travelers following a series of sophisticated cyberattacks targeting guest Wi-Fi networks at hotels and hospitality venues worldwide. The internet hijacking campaign, dubbed ‘CaptiveCrunch’, has been active since at least May and is attributed to Storm-2945, a sub-cluster claimed to be of the Russian hacking group Midnight Blizzard (also known as APT29 or Cozy Bear).According to Microsoft, the hacker group is executing "widespread but targeted" traffic manipulation attacks through Public guest networks and captive portal screens – the web pages that appear when users attempt to log onto hotel Wi-Fi or those at public places like airports, tourists venues and more. "To date, Microsoft has identified widespread compromise of Wi-Fi networks at hospitality-related organizations and other networks serviced by captive portal equipment in several countries. ReliaQuest has identified this activity not only at hotels, but also conference centers and other shared venues, and assesses that the goal of this activity is to access the accounts of corporate travelers," said Microsoft in its report.The hackers compromise the underlying Wi-Fi infrastructure of hospitality venues, redirecting unsuspecting guests through fake portals and malicious pop-ups. Once connected, victims are tricked into downloading malicious files or entering sensitive credentials under the guise of routine security checks.Fake Browser Updates: Guests attempting to connect to hotel Wi-Fi may be presented with pop-ups prompting them to update their web browser or run network troubleshooting utilities. Some prompts mimic official Google security checks with warnings such as: "Our systems have detected unusual traffic from your computer network. Please complete the security check to access Google Search."Account Takeovers: In other instances, users are redirected to convincing fake login screens. Once credentials are submitted, the attackers gain access to the victim's Microsoft 365 accounts, granting them entry to private emails, OneDrive documents, and corporate networks.Once malware is installed on a target device, the hijackers gain broad control. Microsoft warned that Storm-2945 can capture keystrokes, record audio and video, take screenshots, steal browser cookies and stored passwords, and remotely operate the infected device.Microsoft listed a number of potential fake windows that may pop up upon logging into a compromised network, prompting users to download updates or patches. They include:* "winupdate": A Windows Update screen displaying the words "Working on updates… Don't turn off your computer"* "defender": A fake Windows Security virus scan* "directx": A "DirectX End-User Runtime Web Installer"* "vcredist": A Microsoft Visual C++ 2015-2022 Redistributable installer* "sysopt": A disk optimization utility* "netfix": A false Windows Network Diagnostics tool* "browser": A browser update prompt* "pdfview": A document viewer installerMicrosoft urges both individual travelers and corporate IT departments to exercise extreme caution on public networks, recommending the following protective measures:Use Cellular Hotspots: Avoid public or hotel Wi-Fi networks whenever possible; instead, rely on personal cellular hotspots or encrypted private connections.Ignore Unexpected Pop-Ups: Never download browser updates, security tools, network certificates, or software updates offered directly through hotel captive portals or unexpected browser pop-ups.Limit Data Sharing: Companies should review and restrict the sensitive information employees provide to hospitality providers when traveling or logging onto guest networks.
Article Summary: Microsoft warns travelers of sophisticated cyberattacks targeting guest Wi-Fi networks at hotels and hospitality venues worldwide. The internet hijacking campaign, dubbed ‘CaptiveCrunch’, has been active since at least May and is attributed to Storm-2945, a sub-cluster claimed to be of the Russian hacking group Midnight Blizzard.

Article Title: Regional transport authority (RTA) revises rates for private ambulances in Pune district
Article Text:
AI representative image

Pune:





The regional transport authority (RTA), headed by the Pune district collector, has revised the charges of private ambulances operating in the Pune district. The revised rates were decided during a meeting held last week.According to officials with the Pune Regional Transport Office (RTO), rates for converted Maruti vans have been fixed at Rs 700 for the first 24km or one hour, followed by Rs 16 per km and Rs 125 per hour for waiting. The 24-hour rate has been fixed at Rs 4,000.Similarly, for Maruti Eco/Tata Magic ambulances, the corresponding charges are Rs 900, Rs 17 per km, Rs 125 waiting charge and Rs 4,500 for 24 hours, officials said.For Mahindra Bolero/Force Cruiser ambulances, the rates are Rs 1,200 for the first 24km, Rs 18 per km thereafter, Rs 150 per waiting hour and Rs 6,000 for 24 hours. Force Traveller CNG ambulances will charge Rs 1,500 initially, Rs 22 per km, Rs 175 per waiting hour and Rs 7,000 for 24 hours. For larger Force Tempo Traveller CNG ambulances, the rates have been fixed at Rs 2,500, Rs 30 per km, Rs 250 per waiting hour and Rs 10,000 for 24 hours.“The ambulance operators should clearly inform patients and attendants about applicable charges and should not impose unauthorised additional charges or else they will be fined heavily. Operators are also advised to maintain proper records of trips and charges collected,” an RTO official said.

Article Title: Archaeologists uncover human-shaped stones linked to a mysterious Bronze Age burial site in Britain
Article Text:
Image: La Rochelle University

How a strange discovery is changing what researchers know about Coëby cemetery

The human-shaped stones are what make the site particularly unusual

What the cemetery reveals about Bronze Age ideas of death

Why technology is helping archaeologists revisit ancient landscapes

The mystery of Coëby is far from solved

A Bronze Age burial site in Britain is raising new questions about how prehistoric communities treated their dead after archaeologists identified unusual stone objects shaped in ways that may resemble human bodies. The discovery comes from research into the Coëby cemetery, a prehistoric burial landscape in Lincolnshire that contains a series of burial mounds dating back thousands of years.The unusual stones are among several features that make the site difficult to interpret. Rather than being ordinary pieces of naturally occurring rock, some appear to have been deliberately selected or modified and placed in contexts associated with prehistoric burials.A study titled ‘ Atypical Long Barrows in the Cöeby Neolithic Cemetery (Trédion, Morbihan, France)? The Contribution of Electrical Surveys ’ examined the site using archaeological and geophysical evidence, adding another layer to the mystery surrounding Coëby and the practices of the people who used the cemetery.Coëby is part of a wider prehistoric landscape in Lincolnshire containing monuments and burial sites created during the Bronze Age. Burial mounds were an important feature of prehistoric Britain, but the people who constructed them did not always treat the dead in the same way.Some individuals were buried with objects, while others were cremated and their remains placed in vessels or pits. Across Britain, archaeologists have also found evidence that burial monuments were repeatedly modified, reused and incorporated into later landscapes.The Coëby cemetery provides an opportunity to examine these changing practices because its remains preserve evidence of several prehistoric activities within the same landscape.The recent study, published in Archaeological Prospection, used archaeological investigation to reassess features associated with the cemetery and explore what they might reveal about how the site was constructed and used. The research adds new evidence to the continuing investigation of Coëby's prehistoric remains.Among the most intriguing discoveries are stones whose shapes appear to evoke human forms. Such objects are potentially important because deliberately shaped stones can provide clues about how prehistoric communities represented people, the dead or the human body.However, their interpretation requires caution. A stone that resembles a human figure does not necessarily represent an intentional sculpture. Natural weathering, erosion and the shape of the original stone can sometimes produce surprisingly recognisable forms.This is why archaeologists examine not only an object's appearance but also its archaeological context. Where was it found? Was it deliberately placed? Does it show evidence of modification? Was it associated with a burial or monument? And are similar objects found elsewhere?These questions are particularly important at Coëby because the stones cannot be understood separately from the wider burial landscape.Bronze Age burial monuments were not simply places where bodies were deposited and forgotten. Across prehistoric Britain, burial sites appear to have been spaces where communities returned repeatedly, altered monuments and interacted with the remains of earlier generations.The presence of unusual stones at Coëby may therefore point towards a more complicated relationship with the dead. If the stones were deliberately shaped or selected to resemble human figures, they could potentially have played a symbolic role in ceremonies or commemorative practices.But archaeologists have not established a single explanation for their purpose. The evidence allows several possibilities, and further research will be needed to determine whether the human-like appearance was intentional.Modern archaeological investigations increasingly combine traditional excavation with non-invasive techniques that allow researchers to investigate buried remains without disturbing them.At prehistoric burial sites, this can be especially valuable. Geophysical surveys can reveal buried ditches, pits, mound boundaries and other features that are difficult to see from the surface. Researchers can then compare those results with excavation records and previously recovered objects.The research published in Archaeological Prospection demonstrates how reassessing older archaeological landscapes with modern methods can produce new questions even when the monuments themselves have been known for decades.Rather than treating a prehistoric cemetery as a collection of isolated graves, archaeologists can now examine how its different features relate to one another and reconstruct how people may have moved through and interacted with the landscape.The human-shaped stones are intriguing precisely because they raise more questions than they answer. If prehistoric people intentionally selected or shaped them to resemble human forms, their presence could provide rare evidence for how Bronze Age communities represented the human body outside conventional figurative art.If their shapes are instead the result of natural processes, they still demonstrate how easily modern observers can project familiar forms onto ancient objects.For now, Coëby remains a landscape where the physical evidence offers tantalising clues but few definitive answers. The burial mounds, unusual stones and other archaeological features together suggest that the site had a complex history of use.The new research does not close the mystery. Instead, it makes the cemetery even more interesting by showing how much may still be hidden beneath and around Britain's prehistoric burial monuments.
Article Summary: Discovery comes from research into the Coëby cemetery in Lincolnshire. It contains a series of burial mounds dating back thousands of years. The unusual stones are among several features that make the site difficult to interpret. Some appear to have been deliberately selected or modified and placed in contexts associated with prehistoric burials.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Arthur Schopenhauer: 'Talent hits a target no one else can hit. Genius hits a target no one else can see' and the philosophy behind revolutionary thinking
Article Text:
Arthur Schopenhauer

“Talent hits a target no one else can hit. Genius hits a target no one else can see,”

A lonely philosopher’s view of human ability

The World as Will and Representation

Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung

The philosophy of seeing beyond the self

Knowing the difference between optimization and real innovation

For known problems, use talent. Improve your techniques, learn established methods and practice carefully until you can meet clear goals more effectively.

Improve your techniques, learn established methods and practice carefully until you can meet clear goals more effectively. For problems caused by stagnation, make room for genius. Question basic assumptions, step away from immediate measurements and ask what possibilities are being ignored simply because they do not fit current systems.

An archer steps up to the line, pulls back the bowstring and releases an arrow that hits a bullseye two hundred yards away through thick fog. The crowd applauds the incredible skill needed to make a shot that almost nobody else could manage.Then another marksman steps forward, turns forty-five degrees away from the target range and fires an arrow into an empty part of the forest. Moments later, a target that nobody knew was hanging there falls from a high branch.wrote the German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer.The difference challenges the common idea that talent and genius are simply different levels of the same ability. Talent is a quantitative advantage. It means being extremely good at working within existing rules, tools and systems. Genius is different. It is a qualitative change: the ability to see possibilities that other people do not even recognize.Arthur Schopenhauer published this metaphor in the expanded 1844 edition of), in Chapter 31, titled “On Genius.”In the original German, Schopenhauer wrote: “Das Talent gleicht dem Schützen, der ein Ziel trifft, welches die Uebrigen nicht erreichen können; das Genie dem, der eines trifft, bis zu welchem sie nicht ein Mal zu sehn vermögen.”When Schopenhauer wrote these words in 1844, he was a bitter and largely ignored academic living in Frankfurt. The first edition of his major work, published in late 1818, had been a commercial failure. Many copies were eventually sold as wastepaper. For years, he watched contemporaries such as Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel receive fame, university positions and public admiration, while Schopenhauer’s own university lectures attracted very few students.Schopenhauer believed that talent usually belongs to its own time. A talented person becomes highly skilled at answering questions that society is already asking. Because their abilities fit existing needs, they can receive recognition, money and praise quickly.Genius works differently. Schopenhauer compared it to something like a comet entering an orderly planetary system. Because a genius works toward a goal that other people cannot yet understand, their ideas may be met with silence, confusion or even hostility during their lifetime.To understand this difference, we need to look at Schopenhauer’s larger theory of consciousness. He argued that ordinary human thinking is controlled by what he called the “Will”—a blind and constant drive toward survival, self-interest and reproduction.Talent usually works in service of this Will. A talented person uses a powerful intellect to solve practical problems, win competitions or master an existing craft. Their mind may be extremely sharp, but it remains connected to personal goals and the demands of society.Genius appears when the intellect can temporarily escape these demands. Schopenhauer described genius as the ability to enter a state of “pure contemplation.” In this state, a person becomes deeply objective and temporarily forgets their ego, desires and personal situation in order to see things more clearly.Because the genius is less controlled by immediate practical needs, they can notice fundamental truths, artistic forms or scientific principles that other people overlook.This helps explain why major discoveries can sometimes look strange or even foolish to people living at the time. When Gregor Mendel discovered the basic laws of genetic inheritance through his pea plant experiments in 1866, the scientific world largely ignored his published work. It took about thirty-five years for his findings to receive serious recognition. Mendel had identified important patterns of heredity at a time when biology did not yet have the concepts or language needed to fully understand what he had found.In 2026, Schopenhauer’s distinction remains useful for thinking about business, technology and personal development.Modern culture often mistakes extreme optimization for genius. High-frequency trading systems, machine-learning models that break performance records and highly efficient supply chains can represent extraordinary levels of talent. They hit known targets with speeds and accuracy that ordinary people cannot match.But true genius can change the target itself.Consider the development of personal computing and digital media. While many traditional companies were focused on improving existing systems, researchers such as Alan Kay at Xerox PARC were imagining graphical user interfaces, object-oriented programming and portable computers. These ideas went beyond simply making existing tools faster or more efficient. They suggested entirely different ways of interacting with technology.Schopenhauer’s idea can therefore help us decide what kind of thinking a problem requires.Talent is the ability to hit a target that others struggle to reach. Genius is the ability to notice that there is another target altogether.Schopenhauer understood that talent often receives quick recognition because it solves the problems of its own time. Genius is different. It may produce ideas that seem useless, strange or impossible at first because society does not yet know what to do with them.The genius therefore works ahead of the crowd, aiming at something that others cannot yet see. Recognition may come much later, when the world finally catches up with the target.
Article Summary: Arthur Schopenhauer: Talent is a quantitative advantage. Genius is a qualitative change: the ability to see possibilities that other people do not even recognize. A talented person becomes highly skilled at answering questions that society is already asking. Genius appears when the intellect can temporarily escape these demands.

Article Title: Spain's blood-red Río Tinto river is as acidic as vinegar, and Nasa says it could help scientists find life on Mars
Article Text:
PC: David Santiago Garcia/Aurora Photos/Getty Images

Why Spain's Río Tinto river is naturally blood red and as acidic as vinegar

How extremophiles thrive in Spain's highly acidic Río Tinto river

How 5,000 years of mining shaped Spain's famous blood-red river

Why Nasa studies Spain's Río Tinto river to search for life on Mars

At first glance, the Río Tinto in southwestern Spain looks almost unreal. For around 50 kilometres, the water flows in shades of deep red and orange that seem more fitting for an artist's palette than a natural river. Yet its extraordinary appearance is not the result of artificial dyes or recent contamination. It reflects a landscape shaped by ancient geology, microscopic organisms and thousands of years of mining. What appears to be an environment too harsh to support life has instead become home to specialised microbes that thrive where most living things cannot. According to Nasa, those unusual conditions make the Río Tinto one of the closest natural environments on Earth to parts of Mars, giving scientists a rare opportunity to test how they might one day detect life beyond our planet.The Río Tinto, whose name translates as "stained river", cuts through one of Europe's richest volcanic sulfide ore regions. These mineral deposits formed hundreds of millions of years ago when volcanic activity dominated what is now southern Spain.As groundwater and oxygen reach those buried sulfide minerals, a chain of chemical reactions begins. Iron and sulfur compounds dissolve into the water, making it highly acidic.Bacterial communities living within the river do not simply tolerate these conditions, they actively contribute to them by oxidising iron and sulfur compounds. In doing so, they produce ferric iron, the rust-coloured material responsible for the river's striking red appearance.The river's acidity is remarkable. Its pH can fall to around 2, roughly comparable with vinegar, creating an environment where most familiar plants, fish and other aquatic organisms struggle to survive.Despite those hostile conditions, the Río Tinto is far from lifeless. Instead, it supports communities of extremophiles, organisms specially adapted to environments that would prove fatal to most other forms of life. These microbes obtain energy by processing iron and sulfur rather than relying on sunlight or organic matter in the way many other ecosystems do. Their activity also reinforces the river's unusual chemistry, maintaining the acidic conditions that define the ecosystem.Scientists regard these organisms as particularly valuable because they demonstrate that life can flourish in places once thought too extreme to support it. Rather than seeing acidity as an obstacle, these microbes have evolved to use the river's unusual chemical environment as part of their survival strategy.Although the Río Tinto's chemistry has natural origins, people have influenced the landscape for millennia. Archaeological evidence indicates mining in the region stretches back around 5,000 years, spanning the Copper Age, Bronze Age and later Roman activity. Centuries of excavation exposed increasing amounts of sulfide-rich rock to air and water, amplifying processes that were already occurring naturally. Modern industrial mining continued until operations were suspended in 2001 before copper production resumed in 2016.For many years, the river's unusual colour was widely attributed solely to mining pollution. As per the BBC, scientific research has since shown the river's distinctive appearance largely reflects its naturally acidic geochemistry, although extensive mining has intensified those underlying reactions by exposing more mineral deposits.The Río Tinto has become much more than a geological curiosity. Astrobiologists view it as one of Earth's best natural laboratories for testing ideas about extraterrestrial life.The surrounding landscape contains abundant jarosite, an iron- and potassium-rich sulfate mineral that has also been identified on Mars. Because these minerals can preserve traces of microbial activity, scientists believe they could offer clues about where evidence of ancient or even present-day life might survive on the Red Planet.Nasa has used the Río Tinto as a testing ground for robotic life-detection technologies designed for future planetary missions. BBC Travel reports that researchers working beneath the river have discovered diverse microbial communities living underground, strengthening the idea that if life ever developed on Mars, its most promising refuge today may lie beneath the planet's surface rather than on its exposed landscape. For scientists searching beyond Earth, the river offers something rare: a place where extreme chemistry, resilient microorganisms and Martian-like minerals come together in one natural setting.
Article Summary: Spain's Río Tinto river is naturally blood red and as acidic as vinegar. It is one of the closest natural environments on Earth to parts of Mars. Astrobiologists view it as one of Earth's best natural laboratories for testing ideas about extraterrestrial life.

Article Title: Meet Japan’s ‘women of the sea’: 80-year-old diver dives into cold waters without an oxygen tank to harvest seafood using a centuries-old tradition
Article Text:
Image: Metropolis Japan

Japan’s ‘women of the sea’ dive without oxygen tanks

The tradition dates back thousands of years

Award-winning photograph by Kaho Wong, 2017

An 80-year-old Ama became a symbol of the tradition

What do Ama divers collect from the sea?

Their work depends on knowing the sea

Modern Ama still use relatively simple equipment

The number of Ama divers is falling

Some communities are struggling to find younger divers

Changes in the ocean add another challenge

For generations, women along Japan’s Ise-Shima coastline have entered the sea without scuba equipment or oxygen tanks to gather seafood from the seabed. Known as Ama, or ‘women of the sea’, these traditional free divers rely on breath-holding, years of experience and an intimate knowledge of the ocean. Some have continued the demanding work well into their 70s and 80s. In 2012, The Japan Times profiled Reiko Nomura, an 80-year-old former Ama diver in Osatsu, Mie Prefecture, who had spent most of her life diving for abalone and other sea creatures. Today, the tradition survives mainly in coastal communities, although the number of active Ama continues to decline.Ama, a Japanese term commonly translated as ‘woman of the sea’, are traditional female free divers who collect marine life directly from coastal waters. Unlike scuba divers, they do not carry air tanks. They dive on a breath, search the seabed and return to the surface before taking another breath.Japan’s National Tourism Organization says experienced Ama can free-dive to around 15 metres and hold their breath for up to about 60 seconds. Their catches can include abalone, turban shells, sea urchins, sea cucumbers and seaweed.The practice is particularly associated with Toba and Shima in Mie Prefecture, where many of Japan’s remaining Ama continue to work.Ise-Shima’s coastline, with its bays and rich marine environment, has provided the setting for this distinctive fishing culture for generations.Ama diving is frequently described as a tradition dating back more than 3,000 years. Japan’s tourism authorities describe the practice as being part of the country’s ocean-fishing culture for three to five thousand years, while other official material places its documented history more conservatively, noting references to Ama in the eighth-century Man’yoshu poetry collection.This means the safest description is that Ama diving is an ancient tradition with thousands of years of history, rather than claiming that today's exact diving practices have remained unchanged for precisely 3,000 years.The knowledge required for the work has traditionally been passed from one generation to another. Experienced divers learn how to recognise productive areas, understand changing sea conditions and harvest marine life without exhausting local resources.One of the best-documented elderly Ama divers is Reiko Nomura, who was profiled by The Japan Times in 2012 at the age of 80.Nomura grew up surrounded by Ama culture in Osatsu, a coastal village in Mie Prefecture. According to the report, she began diving when she was about 10 and spent most of her life beneath the waves, collecting abalone and other sea creatures.However, there is an important detail often lost in social-media versions of her story. Nomura was no longer actively diving when she was profiled at 80. The Japan Times reported that she had stopped diving a few years earlier and was working as a host at an Ama hut.She nevertheless remained closely connected to the tradition, welcoming visitors, preparing food and sharing stories about her decades as a diver.Ama catches vary according to the location and season, but the seafood associated with the tradition includes abalone, turban shells, sea urchins, sea cucumbers and spiny lobster.Seaweed is also an important part of the traditional catch. Japan’s National Tourism Organization says Ama divers gather various types of seaweed alongside shellfish and other marine products.Abalone has a particularly important place in the culture of the Ise-Shima region. Fresh abalone and turban shells harvested by Ama have even been used as sacred offerings connected with Ise Jingu.Ama diving is not simply a matter of swimming underwater and collecting whatever can be found.The divers depend on detailed knowledge of the coastline, seabed and marine life. They also have to judge weather and sea conditions before entering the water.Traditional fishing rules are designed to prevent excessive harvesting. Restrictions can determine which species may be collected, their size, the fishing season and how long divers can remain in particular areas.The system reflects a long-standing understanding that the Ama communities depend on the same marine resources year after year. Japan’s tourism authorities describe the practice as a form of traditional sustainable fishing in the Ise-Shima region.The image of an Ama diver wearing only traditional white clothing is strongly associated with the culture, but modern Ama generally use equipment suited to contemporary conditions.Many now wear wetsuits, goggles and fins. The breathing method, however, remains fundamentally different from scuba diving because they do not rely on an air tank.Traditional photographs often show divers wearing white garments and carrying simple equipment. The clothing has become an important cultural symbol, even though working divers today commonly use modern protective gear.The culture does not end when the divers return from the water.In places such as Osatsu, visitors can meet Ama at traditional huts where they rest, warm themselves and prepare seafood. Some of these experiences allow visitors to hear directly from the divers about their lives and work.At Ama Hut Hachiman in Toba, visitors can watch Ama prepare and grill seafood such as abalone and spiny lobster while learning about their traditional way of life.The huts have therefore become an important part of cultural tourism while also providing a way for the remaining Ama to share their knowledge with people from outside their communities.Behind the fascinating images of elderly women diving into the sea is a serious concern for the future of the tradition.The number of Ama has fallen sharply over the past several decades. Japan’s National Tourism Organization says there were about 9,100 Ama across Japan in 1978, compared with roughly 2,000 today. It says around half of the remaining Ama are concentrated around the Shima and Toba areas of the Shima Peninsula.The figures vary depending on the geographical area and how active divers are counted, but the long-term decline is clear.An ageing workforce is one of the biggest challenges. Younger women are increasingly choosing other careers, while older Ama eventually retire from the physically demanding work.The problem is particularly visible in some smaller coastal communities.Reuters reported in 2024 that the number of Ama in the Shirahama district of Minamiboso had fallen to 40 in 2023, down 70% from 2006. Their average age had increased from 68 to 72 during that period.The work can be physically demanding and relatively poorly paid, making it difficult to persuade younger people to take it up as a livelihood.Still, there are women trying to keep the practice alive. Reuters reported that Ayumi Inoue, who was 51 at the time, had trained to become an Ama after growing up watching older women in her community practise the tradition.The decline in the number of divers is not the only threat.Ama communities also depend directly on the health of coastal ecosystems. Changes in marine resources can affect the species they traditionally harvest and make the work less predictable.Japan’s tourism authorities have highlighted the decline in ocean resources as another major concern for Ama communities. As the availability of marine life changes, the economic viability of traditional free-diving becomes more difficult.For the Ama, the loss of marine resources can therefore threaten both their livelihoods and the cultural practices associated with them.Despite these pressures, Ama diving has not disappeared.Japan’s National Parks service says there are still more than 600 Ama working in Mie, while Toba and Shima remain the heartland of the tradition.The remaining divers continue to enter the water using breath-hold techniques that have been passed down through generations. Some work well into their later years, while others eventually move into roles that allow them to share their knowledge without continuing the physical demands of diving.
Article Summary: Ama, a Japanese term commonly translated as ‘woman of the sea’, are traditional female free divers who collect marine life directly from coastal waters. Unlike scuba divers, they do not carry air tanks. They dive on a breath, search the seabed and return to the surface before taking another breath. Their catches can include abalone, turban shells, sea cucumbers and seaweed.

Article Title: In 1976, a 26-year-old biologist camped alone beneath a 35-foot artificial eagle nest: One chick she raised went on to father around 70 more
Article Text:
AI REPRESENTATION: The goal was to use a technique known as hacking, in which young birds are raised in a controlled setting before being released to live independently | ChatGPT

AI REPRESENTATION: The goal was to use a technique known as hacking, in which young birds are raised in a controlled setting before being released to live independently | ChatGPT

The eagles had to learn to live without people

What made M3 so special?

Bald eagle | Wikimedia Commons

A species once down to 417 nesting pairs

Tina Morris was 26 years old when she spent months living alone beside an artificial nest at New York's Montezuma National Wildlife Refuge. Her job was to raise young bald eagles and see whether they could survive after being released into the wild. The experiment began in 1976, when the species was still struggling after decades of persecution, habitat loss and the effects of DDT. Morris was a graduate student at Cornell's Laboratory of Ornithology when she was selected for the project. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service says she eventually spent two years working with seven eaglets at Montezuma, near Seneca Falls, New York.The young eagles lived in a man-made nest about 35 feet above the ground, while Morris stayed nearby and watched them from a concealed position. She did not have a lot of experience caring for eagles and was also afraid of heights. Each day, she climbed the tower to provide food without allowing the birds to become dependent on human contact. The goal was to use a technique known as hacking, in which young birds are raised in a controlled setting before being released to live independently. The method had been used with other raptors, but applying it to bald eagles was still an experiment.Morris could not simply feed the eaglets by hand because regular contact with people could lead to imprinting. The young birds needed to develop normal associations with their own species rather than treating humans as a source of food. Morris therefore stayed out of sight and used a long stick to place food inside the artificial nest. She collected roadkill when available and caught carp, then attached a barbecue fork to the end of the stick. The setup allowed her to feed the birds without standing directly beside them. She also spent time observing their behavior and recording how they responded to the nest, food and surrounding environment. Once the eaglets began leaving the tower, her work shifted to tracking them and checking where they landed.The first two eaglets arrived from Wisconsin in June 1976. They were identified as W1 and W2 and became the first birds in Morris's care at the artificial nesting site. A third eagle, M3, arrived later after being found in Michigan with a broken leg. His injury had already been treated before he joined the group. M3 had experienced contact with people, unlike the first two birds, but he had not become imprinted on humans. Morris later recalled that she became particularly attached to him during the rehabilitation effort. The three birds gave her an opportunity to observe how young bald eagles behaved as they developed outside a conventional nest and prepared for their first flights.The transition from the tower to the surrounding refuge required close monitoring. Young eagles do not immediately have the flight control needed for long distances or safe landings, so Morris followed their movements after they left the nest. Some landed in places where they could not easily return to the tower. One bird ended up in a marsh and had to be carried back. Morris also had to search for birds that disappeared from view and check on them after difficult landings. Much of the work involved routine tasks rather than dramatic moments: preparing food, climbing the tower, watching the birds, recording their behavior and searching the refuge when an eaglet could no longer be seen. Those daily observations became an important part of the hands-on work behind the project.The first group eventually left the area as independent birds. Morris returned to the project in 1977, when she helped raise another four eaglets. By then, the basic approach had proved workable, and other researchers became involved. The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation later took over the program.M3's story continued even after Morris's time at Montezuma ended. The eagle was identified by his band number, 03142, and eventually settled in New York. He lived for about 35 years and fathered an estimated 70 offspring, according to accounts of Morris's research and memoir. Morris did not initially know that the eagle was M3; she sadly learned his identity after the bird was killed by a vehicle while feeding on roadkill.The figure of 70 should be treated as an estimate rather than a precise count. It refers to chicks that are attributed to M3 during his life, not to 70 descendants across multiple generations. His story nevertheless gave Morris an unusually direct link to the long-term results of the experiment she had worked on as a young biologist.The bald eagle's situation in the United States was far more serious when Morris began her work. In 1963, only 417 known nesting pairs remained in the lower 48 states, according to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service . DDT was a major factor, which accumulated through the food chain and interfered with the birds' ability to produce strong eggshells. Habitat loss, shooting and other pressures had also reduced populations.The species eventually made a major recovery. In 2007, the Fish and Wildlife Service removed the bald eagle from the federal endangered and threatened species list after determining that populations in the lower 48 had recovered. The agency estimated 9,789 breeding pairs at the time. A later federal estimate based on 2018-2019 data put the population at about 316,700 individual bald eagles, including 71,467 breeding pairs.Laws protecting eagles, the U.S. ban on DDT, habitat protection and other conservation programs all played major roles. But the work at Montezuma helped establish a practical method for releasing young bald eagles into areas where the species had disappeared. Nearly five decades later, the experiment is preserved not only in conservation records but also in the story of M3, one of the eaglets Morris once watched from a hidden position beside a 35-foot nest.
Article Summary: Tina Morris was 26 years old when she spent months living alone beside an artificial nest at New York's Montezuma National Wildlife Refuge. Her job was to raise young bald eagles and see whether they could survive after being released into the wild. The goal was to use a technique known as hacking, in which young birds are raised in a controlled setting before being released to live independently.

Article Title: North Carolina dam tested three water flows for 20 years, and scientists found the level that protects river wildlife while keeping more water for power
Article Text:
Image AI generated

Why did Roanoke Rapids Dam change the river's water flow

Why did scientists choose the medium flow level

How will medium water flow help generate more electricity

What can other hydroelectric operators learn from North Carolina's Roanoke Rapids Dam

A North Carolina hydroelectric dam has spent two decades testing how much water it can hold back without harming the wildlife downstream. The Roanoke Rapids Dam, run by Dominion Energy, diverts most of the Roanoke River's flow through a powerhouse channel to generate electricity, leaving a bypassed stretch of the original riverbed with reduced water. Since 2004, under the terms of its federal licence, operators have trialled three flow levels, low, medium and high, while researchers tracked the response of American shad, American eels and freshwater mussels living in that stretch. The results, published after monitoring in 2024 and 2025, have now given engineers a clear operational answer for the remaining 18 years of the dam's licence, ending years of uncertainty over how to balance power output with species protection. The findings offer a rare, data-driven resolution to a debate that has long divided energy producers and conservationists, showing that sustained, patient research can uncover practical solutions where power generation and ecological protection once seemed fundamentally at odds.The long-term experiment effectively turned the bypassed river section into a real-world testing ground for environmental management.Rather than relying on short-term observations, researchers were able to compare biological responses across different flow conditions over many years, providing stronger evidence for deciding how much water should remain in the river while the dam continues producing electricity.The Roanoke Rapids Dam has diverted the majority of the river's downstream flow into an engineered channel since it was built, cutting off a section of the natural riverbed known as the bypassed reach. This reduced flow altered the habitat available to fish and mussels that depend on moving water to navigate, feed and spawn. When the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission renewed the dam's operating licence in 2004, it required Dominion Energy to work with NOAA Fisheries and other state and federal resource agencies on a new, multi-staged water release pattern for this section of river.The plan called for three flow levels, tested in stages across the first 20 years of the licence, with regular surveys built into the licence terms to record how fish and mussels responded to each setting. This structure gave researchers a long runway to gather reliable data rather than relying on short-term observations, allowing conclusions to be drawn from sustained population trends instead of isolated survey results.According to NOAA Fisheries, scientists evaluated all three flow levels during the 2024 and 2025 monitoring period and found that shad, eel and mussel populations increased under both the medium and high flow patterns compared with the low flow level. Low flow settings kept the most water behind the dam for power generation, but the reduced habitat availability under this setting corresponded with limited fish movement and weaker mussel health in the bypassed reach. However, the benefits of the high flow setting were not significantly different from those recorded under the medium setting, meaning the extra water released at the high level produced no measurable additional gain for wildlife. This was the key finding that shaped the final decision, since it demonstrated that pushing more water through the bypassed reach beyond a certain point simply diverted resources away from electricity generation without improving conditions for shad, eels or mussels.According to NOAA Fisheries, this allowed more water to be diverted to the powerhouse for electricity generation without any negative impact on the fish and mussel populations being monitored. The agency notes that Dominion Energy will now use the medium flow pattern for the remaining 18 years of the dam's hydroelectric licence, a decision reached jointly with state and federal resource agencies after reviewing the full set of survey results gathered over the monitoring period.With the medium flow confirmed as sufficient for wildlife, Dominion Energy can direct more water towards electricity production during periods of peak demand while still meeting the habitat needs of migratory species during breeding and migration windows. This arrangement removes much of the guesswork that previously surrounded flow management at the dam, replacing it with a fixed operational target supported by nearly two decades of field data. The medium flow pattern is expected to remain in place for the rest of the current licence term, giving both the utility and the surrounding ecosystem a stable baseline rather than a setting subject to ongoing review or renegotiation.The Roanoke Rapids case offers a practical model for other hydroelectric operators facing similar licensing reviews, particularly those balancing energy demands with obligations to protect migratory fish and freshwater mussels. Rather than treating power output and species protection as competing priorities, the long-term monitoring programme identified the exact point at which additional water release stopped delivering ecological benefit.That threshold now forms the basis of a long-term operating plan, giving both the utility and resource agencies a stable, data-backed reference point for the remainder of the dam's licence, and demonstrating how sustained collaboration between industry and regulators can produce outcomes that serve both energy needs and river health.
Article Summary: North Carolina's Roanoke Rapids Dam has spent two decades testing how much water it can hold back without harming the wildlife downstream. Since 2004, under the terms of its federal licence, operators have trialled three flow levels, low, medium and high. Researchers tracked the response of American shad, American eels and freshwater mussels living in that stretch. Results have now given engineers a clear operational answer for the remaining 18 years of the dam's licence.

Article Title: Scientists build a silicon chip that writes DNA with electricity, paving the way for cleaner gene synthesis and DNA-based data storage
Article Text:
Representative image

How the silicon chip works

From neuroscience to biotechnology

Potential applications

Challenges ahead

Silicon chips have long been the backbone of computing, but a Harvard-led research team has given them an entirely different job: writing DNA. As reported by Science Daily, a study published in Nature Electronics, Harvard researchers have unveiled a silicon chip DNA writer capable of synthesising DNA using electricity and water-based enzymes. The innovation marks a major departure from traditional phosphoramidite chemistry, which relies on hazardous organic solvents. The chip can simultaneously produce 64 different DNA sequences, each up to 39 nucleotides long, offering a cleaner and more scalable approach to DNA manufacturing.The project involved Harvard, the Broad Institute, DNA Script, and POSTECH, with funding from IARPA, Horizon Europe, and Samsung Research. Intellectual property has been filed by Harvard’s Office of Technology Development.The chip assembles DNA strands one nucleotide at a time. A temporary blocking group halts growth until removed under acidic conditions. By applying tiny electrical currents, the chip generates protons that lower pH locally, enabling DNA synthesis to continue. Each site is confined by concentric ring electrodes, allowing parallel construction of multiple sequences.This precise control makes the process safer and more efficient than conventional methods.Synthetic DNA is essential for diagnostics, genome engineering, and cancer research. Current methods require centralized facilities and involve toxic solvents. The Harvard chip’s water-based enzymatic process could enable portable DNA-writing devices, making the technology more accessible to labs and clinics worldwide.Interestingly, the chip’s design originated in neuroscience research, where it was used to record electrical activity in neurons. Researchers later repurposed its precision current injection technology to control chemical conditions for DNA synthesis, bridging the gap between brain science and biotechnology.* Portable DNA-writing devices for labs and hospitals* DNA data storage, demonstrated by encoding a 169-byte text* Synthetic biology and diagnostics with reduced environmental impactScaling the technology will require new chemistry. Current limitations stem from intermediate molecules drifting between synthesis sites during deprotection. Researchers are working on more direct acid-driven chemistry to overcome this hurdle, aiming for longer and more complex DNA sequences.

The innovation marks a major departure from traditional phosphoramidite chemistry, which relies on hazardous organic solvents. The chip can simultaneously produce 64 different DNA sequences, each up to 39 nucleotides long.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.
